title: Meiosis
short: Meiosis is two divisions that turn one diploid cell into four haploid cells. Meiosis I separates homologous pairs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
trouble: Students think meiosis II halves the chromosome number again, or that meiosis I separates sister chromatids. The number halves in meiosis I, when homologs part; meiosis II is like mitosis.

blocks.html: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same. But gametes must carry half the number: when two gametes combine, the new cell has two sets again. Meiosis is the cell division that makes those haploid cells.
Meiosis is two divisions that turn one diploid cell into four haploid cells. Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, halving the chromosome number. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis.

blocks.cap: Where the number halves: anaphase I.

blocks.html: The difference from mitosis is in metaphase I. In mitosis, chromosomes line up one by one; in meiosis I, they line up in pairs, each homolog facing a different pole. When the pairs split, each new cell gets one chromosome of each pair: a full single set, $n$. Each of those chromosomes is still two chromatids, so meiosis II splits them, exactly like mitosis, without copying the DNA again in between.

blocks.title: Count through meiosis
blocks.q: A cell with $2n = 8$ goes through meiosis. How many chromosomes are in each cell after meiosis I, and after meiosis II?
steps: Meiosis I separates the 4 homologous pairs: each of two cells gets 4 chromosomes (each still two chromatids).
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids: each of four cells gets 4 chromosomes of one chromatid.
The number halved once, from 8 to 4, in meiosis I.
blocks.a: 4 after meiosis I; 4 after meiosis II (in four cells)

blocks.html: Thinking meiosis II halves the number again, or that meiosis I separates sister chromatids. The number halves only once, in meiosis I, when homologs part. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis, so the number of chromosomes per cell stays at $n$. Check with humans: 46 in, 23 per cell after meiosis I, still 23 after meiosis II.
